args.title: deviation-analysis-memo.docx
args.body:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
MEMORANDUM

TO: Engagement Team
FROM: Banking & Finance Practice Group
RE: Counterparty Markup Deviation Analysis — Senior Secured Credit Facility Term Sheet
DATE: [Date]

I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This memorandum analyzes the lender's markup of the Senior Secured Credit Facility term sheet against the original term sheet (the "Base Materials"), cross-referencing (i) the firm's deviation review playbook, (ii) the controlling partner instructions on the engagement, and (iii) the applicable financial data and disclosure schedules. The objective is to identify each deviation introduced by the counterparty markup, assess its materiality, reconcile it against the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and recommend an accept/reject/concede position consistent with the governing client direction.

II. MATERIALS REVIEWED

1. Base deal materials (doc. 3) — original Senior Secured Credit Facility term sheet, including representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination provisions negotiated between the parties.
2. Counterparty markup (doc. 29) — the lender's revision, which accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three substantive deviations.
3. Schedules and exhibits (doc. 81) — disclosure schedules qualifying the base materials: Schedule 3.7 (pending regulatory inquiries), Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities), and Exhibit B (survival matrix).
4. Deal correspondence / partner instructions (doc. 107) — partner email thread on the engagement. The controlling instruction is the latest message: the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue.
5. An unrelated administrative correspondence file was misfiled into the matter folder (doc. 55) and was disregarded; it is not relied upon for this analysis.

III. GOVERNING CLIENT/PARTNER DIRECTION

The latest partner message on the engagement is controlling and supersedes any earlier, contradictory statements in the thread:
- The client WILL CONCEDE the basket conversion (conversion of the indemnification deductible to a tipping basket).
- Any reduction of the survival period for the core representations is a WALK-AWAY issue — the client will not accept a shortened survival period.

The deviation analysis below applies these instructions to each markup change.

IV. DEVIATION ANALYSIS

Deviation 1 — Indemnification Cap Reduction and Basket Conversion (Deductible → Tipping Basket)

Markup change: The counterparty markup (i) silently reduces the indemnification cap and (ii) converts the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket.

Analysis:
- Basket conversion. As directed by the controlling partner instruction, the client has agreed to concede the conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket. On that instruction, the basket conversion is treated as a conceded point and is not a walk-away issue. However, the concession does not cure the separate cap reduction, which must be analyzed independently.
- Cap reduction. The silent reduction of the indemnification cap is a material and commercially adverse deviation. It is particularly problematic when read together with Schedule 5.2, which lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift onto the client. Reducing the cap while converting to a tipping basket, combined with the retained-liability carryover under Schedule 5.2, materially increases the client's exposure and shifts risk that the parties had not agreed to allocate. The scheduled exceptions in Schedule 5.2 control over the general statements in the base materials, so the retained liabilities must remain within the agreed indemnification framework.
- Recommendation: Reject the silent reduction of the indemnification cap. The client's concession on the basket conversion should not be read as a concession on the cap amount. The cap as originally set in the base materials should be preserved, and Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities must remain covered.

Deviation 2 — Material Adverse Effect (MAE) Carve-Outs for Regulatory Action

Markup change: The markup's definition of Material Adverse Effect adds carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter.

Analysis:
- Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries. These inquiries intersect directly with the MAE carve-outs introduced by the markup. If accepted, the carve-outs would carve out precisely the regulatory actions currently under inquiry, potentially excluding from the MAE definition events that the parties had agreed would constitute a material adverse change. The scheduled exception in Schedule 3.7 indicates the client has already disclosed these inquiries; the counterparty's carve-out would undermine the protective effect of the MAE definition in the very scenario that is live.
- Recommendation: Reject the MAE carve-outs for regulatory action. Because the markup carves out "regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter" (the two pending inquiries in Schedule 3.7), accepting it would strip the MAE representation of its intended coverage at the point of greatest risk. The MAE definition should remain as set out in the base materials, without the regulatory-action carve-out.

Deviation 3 — Limitation Period Shortening Survival for Core Representations

Markup change: A new limitation period shortens the survival period for the core representations.

Analysis:
- Exhibit B of the base materials sets the survival matrix for the representations. The markup's new limitation period directly contradicts the survival matrix in Exhibit B by shortening survival for the core representations. The scheduled exception/Exhibit B control over general statements in the base materials; the survival periods in Exhibit B are the operative baseline.
- Controlling partner instruction: Any survival-period reduction is a WALK-AWAY issue. Accordingly, the client will not accept a shortened survival period for the core representations. This is a deal-critical, non-negotiable point.
- Recommendation: Walk away / refuse the survival-period reduction. The survival periods for the core representations must remain as set in Exhibit B. The client treats this as a walk-away issue and will not agree to the shortened limitation period.

V. RECONCILIATION OF SCHEDULES AND EXHIBITS

Per the schedules and exhibits (doc. 81), the scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. Three reconciliations are required:

- Schedule 3.7 (two pending regulatory inquiries) intersects Deviation 2 (MAE carve-outs). The carve-outs must be rejected because they would exclude the exact regulatory actions already disclosed in Schedule 3.7.
- Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities) intersects Deviation 1 (indemnification cap/basket). The cap reduction and basket changes would silently shift retained liabilities; these must be corrected so Schedule 5.2 liabilities remain within the agreed indemnification framework.
- Exhibit B (survival matrix) intersects Deviation 3 (limitation period). The shortened limitation period contradicts Exhibit B and is a walk-away issue.

VI. CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDED POSITION

Summary of deviations and recommended positions:

| # | Deviation | Recommended Position |
|---|-----------|----------------------|
| 1a | Basket conversion (deductible → tipping) | CONCEDE (per partner instruction) |
| 1b | Indemnification cap reduction | REJECT — preserve original cap; Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities must remain covered |
| 2 | MAE carve-outs for regulatory action | REJECT — carve-outs cover the exact pending inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7 |
| 3 | Limitation period shortening survival of core representations | WALK AWAY — survival periods must remain per Exhibit B |

The counterparty markup's most serious deviations are the silent reduction of the indemnification cap (which, together with the basket conversion and Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities, shifts additional risk to the client) and the shortened survival period for core representations (a walk-away issue per the controlling partner instruction). The MAE carve-outs must also be rejected because they would neutralize material adverse effect coverage in the very regulatory scenario pending under Schedule 3.7.

The client may concede the basket conversion as directed, but the firm should hold firm on the indemnification cap, the MAE carve-outs, and — most critically — the survival period for the core representations.

Prepared for internal use and at the direction of the engagement partner.

Confidential — Attorney Work Product / Privileged. This memorandum is prepared in anticipation of litigation and in connection with legal representation.
